takeaway: Meckel's diverticulum: dark-red rectal bleeding and pallor in a young boy, from a remnant of the vitelline duct.

question.text: A 2-year-old boy presents with dark-red rectal bleeding and general pallor. There has been no vomiting and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Select the likely diagnosis.
question.say: A two-year-old boy presents with dark-red rectal bleeding and general pallor. There has been no vomiting, and abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the likely diagnosis?

lines.say: This little two-year-old boy looks pale and worried.
His nappy shows dark-red rectal bleeding. That explains the pallor.

lines.text: No vomiting, and a normal abdomen.
lines.say: But there is no vomiting, and his abdomen feels normal. So no obstruction.

lines.text: The culprit: a small pouch off the small bowel.
lines.say: The culprit is this cheerful pouch, Meckel's diverticulum, the most common congenital anomaly of the small intestine.

lines.text: It is a leftover of the vitelline duct.
lines.say: It comes from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline duct. About two per cent of people have one, more often males.

lines.text: Remember: dark-red rectal bleeding and pallor in a toddler is Meckel's diverticulum.
lines.say: Remember: dark-red rectal bleeding and pallor in a toddler, with a quiet abdomen, mean Meckel's diverticulum.
